# Migrate from 7.x to 8.x

## Learn about migrating from Sentry JavaScript SDK 7.x to 8.x

The main goal of version 8 is to improve our performance monitoring APIs, integrations API, and ESM support. This version is breaking because we removed deprecated APIs, restructured npm package contents, and introduced new dependencies on OpenTelemetry.

## 

Before updating to `8.x` of the SDK, we recommend upgrading to the latest version of `7.x`. To fix most of the deprecations on `7.x`, you can use the `@sentry/migr8` codemod to automatically update your SDK usage. `@sentry/migr8` requires Node 18+.

[Button: Bash]

``

Copied
    
    `npx @sentry/migr8@latest
    `

Our migration tool will let you select which updates to run, and automatically update your code. In some cases, we cannot automatically change code for you. These will be marked with a `TODO(sentry)` comment instead. Make sure to review all code changes after running `@sentry/migr8`! For more details on the deprecations, see our docs on Deprecations in 7.x. Despite having `@sentry/migr8`, we still recommend reading the migration guide, since `@sentry/migr8` does not cover all of the changes needed to migrate.

## 

`8.x` simplifies Sentry SDK initialization and makes several internal improvements.

We recommend you read through all the Important Changes as they affect all SDK users. The Other Changes linked below only affect users who have more customized instrumentation. There is also a Troubleshooting section for common issues.

We also have a detailed migration guide on GitHub, which has a comprehensive list of all changes alongside the source code of the SDK.

## 

### 

The SDK now requires ES2018 compatibility plus support for `globalThis`. The minimum supported browser versions are:

  * Chrome 71
  * Edge 79
  * Safari 12.1, iOS Safari 12.2
  * Firefox 65
  * Opera 58
  * Samsung Internet 10

For IE11 support please transpile your code to ES5 using babel or similar and add required polyfills.

### 

The Custom Instrumentation API for Tracing has been revamped in `8.x`. New methods have been introduced, and `startTransaction` and `span.startChild` has been removed. See the new Tracing APIs docs for more information.

Only `makeFetchTransport` is available now. This means that the Sentry SDK requires the `fetch` API to be available in the environment.

### 

The `Offline` integration has been removed in favor of the offline transport wrapper

### 

The `Sentry.wrap` export has been removed. There is no replacement API.

### 

We updated the behaviour of the SDKs when no `tracePropagationTargets` option was defined. As a reminder, you can provide a list of strings or RegExes that will be matched against URLs to tell the SDK, to which outgoing requests tracing HTTP headers should be attached to. These tracing headers are used for distributed tracing.

Previously, on the browser, when `tracePropagationTargets` were not defined, they defaulted to the following: `['localhost', /^\/(?!\/)/]`. This meant that all request targets to that had "localhost" in the URL, or started with a `/` were equipped with tracing headers. This default was chosen to prevent CORS errors in your browser applications. However, this default had a few flaws.

Going forward, when the `tracePropagationTargets` option is not set, tracing headers will be attached to all outgoing requests on the same origin. For example, if you're on `https://example.com/` and you send a request to `https://example.com/api`, the request will be traced (ie. will have trace headers attached). Requests to `https://api.example.com/` will not, because it is on a different origin. The same goes for all applications running on `localhost`.

When you provide a `tracePropagationTargets` option, all of the entries you defined will now be matched be matched against the full URL of the outgoing request. Previously, it was only matched against what you called request APIs with. For example, if you made a request like `fetch("/api/posts")`, the provided `tracePropagationTargets` were only compared against `"/api/posts"`.


### 

The top level `Sentry.configureScope` function has been removed. Instead, you should use the `Sentry.getCurrentScope()` to access and mutate the current scope.

[Button: JavaScript]

``

Copied
    
    `- Sentry.configureScope((scope) => {
    -  scope.setTag("key", "value");
    - });
    + Sentry.getCurrentScope().setTag("key", "value");
    `

### 

`tracingOrigins` is now removed in favor of the `tracePropagationTargets` option. The `tracePropagationTargets` option should be set in the `Sentry.init()` options, or in your custom `Client`s option if you create them.

[Button: TypeScript]

``

Copied
    
    `Sentry.init({
      dsn: "https://examplePublicKey@o0.ingest.sentry.io/0",
      integrations: [Sentry.browserTracingIntegration()],
      tracePropagationTargets: ["localhost", "example.com"],
    });
    `

### 

In `7.x`, you had to enable the metrics aggregator by setting the `_experiments` option to `{ metricsAggregator: true }`. In addition for browser environments you had to add the `metricsAggregatorIntegration` to the `integrations` array.

[Button: TypeScript]

``

Copied
    
    `
    Sentry.init({
      dsn: "https://examplePublicKey@o0.ingest.sentry.io/0
    
    example-org / example-project
    
    ",
      _experiments: {
        metricsAggregator: true,
      },
    });
    
    
    Sentry.init({
      dsn: "https://examplePublicKey@o0.ingest.sentry.io/0
    
    example-org / example-project
    
    ",
      integrations: [Sentry.metricsAggregatorIntegration()],
    });
    
    Sentry.metrics.increment("my_metric");
    `

In `8.x` no additional configuration is needed to use metrics APIs.

[Button: Ts]

``

Copied
    
    `
    Sentry.init({
      dsn: "https://examplePublicKey@o0.ingest.sentry.io/0
    
    example-org / example-project
    
    ",
    });
    
    Sentry.metrics.increment("my_metric");

## OAuth2

For third-party applications that need to access Sentry on behalf of users, Sentry supports OAuth2 with the authorization code grant type. This allows users to authorize your application without sharing their credentials.

### Authorization Request

Direct users to the authorization endpoint:

[Button: Bash]

``

Copied
    
    `https://sentry.io/oauth/authorize/?client_id={CLIENT_ID}&response_type=code&scope={SCOPES}
    `
    
    `https://sentry.io/oauth/authorize/?client_id={CLIENT_ID}&response_type=code&scope={SCOPES}
    `

Parameters:

Parameter  | Required  | Description
--- | --- | ---
`client_id`  | Yes  | Your registered client ID
`response_type`  | Yes  | Must be `code`
`scope`  | Yes  | Space-separated list of permissions
`redirect_uri`  | No  | Your callback URI (must match registered URI)
`state`  | No  | Random string to prevent CSRF attacks
`code_challenge`  | Recommended  | PKCE challenge (see below)
`code_challenge_method`  | Recommended  | Must be `S256`

After the user approves, Sentry redirects to your callback URI with an authorization code:

[Button: Bash]

``

Copied
    
    `https://your-app.com/callback?code={AUTHORIZATION_CODE}
    `
    
    `https://your-app.com/callback?code={AUTHORIZATION_CODE}
    `

### Token Exchange

Exchange the authorization code for an access token:

[Button: Bash]

``

Copied
    
    `curl -X POST https://sentry.io/oauth/token/ \
      -d client_id={CLIENT_ID} \
      -d client_secret=REDACTED \
      -d grant_type=authorization_code \
      -d code={AUTHORIZATION_CODE} \
      -d code_verifier={CODE_VERIFIER}
    `
    
    `curl -X POST https://sentry.io/oauth/token/ \
      -d client_id={CLIENT_ID} \
      -d client_secret=REDACTED \
      -d grant_type=authorization_code \
      -d code={AUTHORIZATION_CODE} \
      -d code_verifier={CODE_VERIFIER}
    `

The `code_verifier` parameter is required if you used PKCE in the authorization request.

Response:

[Button: JSON]

``

Copied
    
    `{
      "access_token": "{ACCESS_TOKEN}",
      "refresh_token": "{REFRESH_TOKEN}",
      "expires_in": 2591999,
      "expires_at": "2024-11-27T23:20:21.054320Z",
      "token_type": "bearer",
      "scope": "org:read project:read",
      "user": {
        "id": "123",
        "name": "Jane Doe",
        "email": "jane@example.com"
      }
    }

    `{
      "access_token": "{ACCESS_TOKEN}",
      "refresh_token": "{REFRESH_TOKEN}",
      "expires_in": 2591999,
      "expires_at": "2024-11-27T23:20:21.054320Z",
      "token_type": "bearer",
      "scope": "org:read project:read",
      "user": {
        "id": "123",
        "name": "Jane Doe",
        "email": "jane@example.com"
      }
    }
    `

#### Step 2: Display Instructions to User

Display the user code and verification URL to your user:

[Button: Bash]

``

Copied
    
    `To authenticate, visit: https://sentry.io/oauth/device/
    Enter code: ABCD-EFGH
    `
    
    `To authenticate, visit: https://sentry.io/oauth/device/
    Enter code: ABCD-EFGH
    `

The user code uses an unambiguous character set (no 0/O, 1/I/L confusion) for easy entry.

#### Step 3: Poll for Token

While the user authorizes in their browser, poll the token endpoint:

[Button: Bash]

``

Copied
    
    `curl -X POST https://sentry.io/oauth/token/ \
      -d client_id={CLIENT_ID} \
      -d device_code={DEVICE_CODE} \
      -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code
    `

      -d client_id={CLIENT_ID} \
      -d device_code={DEVICE_CODE} \
      -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code

Poll at the `interval` specified in the device authorization response (default: 5 seconds). While waiting for the user, you'll receive:

[Button: JSON]

``

    }

# Permissions & Scopes

If you're building on top of Sentry's API (i.e using Auth Tokens), you'll need certain scopes to access different API endpoints.

To set the scopes for an integration token, select the scopes from the dropdown. These can be edited later.

To set the scopes for an personal token, select the scopes from the dropdown when creating a personal token. These cannot be edited later.

Image

If you're looking for information on membership roles please visit the membership documentation.

### Organizations

 | 
--- | ---
GET  | `org:read`
PUT/POST  | `org:write`
DELETE  | `org:admin`

### Continuous Integration (CI)

 | 
--- | ---
CI Workflows  | `org:ci`

Use the `org:ci` scope for CI and deployment workflows, including uploading source maps, creating releases, and managing code mappings.

### Projects

 | 
--- | ---
GET  | `project:read`
PUT/POST  | `project:write`
DELETE  | `project:admin`

##### Note

The `project:releases` scope will give you access to both project and organization release endpoints. The available endpoints are listed in the Releases section of the API Documentation.

### Teams

 | 
--- | ---
GET  | `team:read`
PUT/POST  | `team:write`
DELETE  | `team:admin`

### Members

 | 
--- | ---
GET  | `member:read`
PUT/POST  | `member:write`
DELETE  | `member:admin`

### Issues & Events

 | 
--- | ---
GET  | `event:read`
PUT  | `event:write`
DELETE  | `event:admin`

##### Note

PUT/DELETE methods only apply to updating/deleting issues. Events in Sentry are immutable and can only be deleted by deleting the whole issue.

### Releases

 | 
--- | ---
GET/PUT/POST/DELETE  | `project:releases`

##### Note

Be aware that if you're using `sentry-cli` to manage your releases, you'll need a token which also has `org:read` scope.

##### Project Access

In addition to the `project:releases` scope, mutations on releases (create, update, delete, file uploads, deploys) require that the user has access to all projects associated with the release. If your organization has Open Membership disabled, members can only modify releases for projects belonging to teams they are a member of.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Requests

All API requests should be made to the `/api/0/` prefix, and will return JSON as the response:

## HTTP Verbs

Sentry makes an attempt to stick to appropriate HTTP verbs, but we always prioritize usability over correctness.

Method  | Description
--- | ---
`DELETE`  | Used for deleting resources.
`GET`  | Used for retrieving resources.
`OPTIONS`  | Describes the given endpoint.
`POST`  | Used for creating resources.
`PUT`  | Used for updating resources. Partial data is accepted where possible.

## Parameters and Data

Any parameters not included in the URL should be encoded as JSON with a Content-Type of `'application/json'`:
    
    `curl -i https://sentry.io/api/0/organizations/acme/projects/1/groups/ \
        -d '{"status": "resolved"}' \
        -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
    `
    
    `curl -i https://sentry.io/api/0/organizations/acme/projects/1/groups/ \
        -d '{"status": "resolved"}' \
        -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
    `

Additional parameters are sometimes specified via the querystring, even for `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` requests:
    
    `curl -i https://sentry.io/api/0/organizations/acme/projects/1/groups/?status=unresolved \
        -d '{"status": "resolved"}' \
        -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
    `--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L70: # R-CLI Overview
L71: 
L72: Install Backboard R-CLI, sign in, open a project, and run your first session in the terminal.
L73: 
L74: Backboard R-CLI is a coding agent that runs in your terminal. Start it inside a project, type what you want, and it can read files, edit files, run commands, use MCP tools, and ask for clarification when needed.
L75: 
L76: This page covers the smallest useful workflow. Once you are comfortable, see 【10†Permissions】 to control what the agent may do, and 【11†Checkpoints】 to undo its file changes.
L77: ## 【50†​】Install Backboard R-CLI
L78: 
L79: Install the `backboard` command for your operating system:
L80: 
L81:   * ## macOS / Linux
L82: 
L83:   * ## Windows PowerShell
L84: 
L85:     `curl -fsSL https://app.backboard.io/api/cli | bash
L86:     `
L87: 
L88: Restart your terminal if the command is not found, then verify the install:
L89: 
L90:     `backboard --version
L91:     backboard --help
L92:     `
L93: 
L94: 【51†Image: Backboard R-CLI help output†storage.googleapis.com】
L95: 
L96: Verify the Backboard R-CLI command is available.
L97: ## 【52†​】Sign in
L98: 
L99: If you start R-CLI before signing in, it will ask you to log in or sign up.
L100: 
L101: 【53†Image: Backboard R-CLI signed out screen†storage.googleapis.com】
L102: 
L103: R-CLI prompts for login when no saved credentials are available.
L104: 
L105: Run:
L106: 
L107:     `backboard login
L108:     `
L109: 
L110: The CLI prints a browser URL, a short code, and a QR code. Either open the URL on this machine, or scan the QR code with your phone to approve the login there. Approve the device login, then return to the terminal.
L111: 【54†Image: Backboard R-CLI login prompt†storage.googleapis.com】
L112: 
L113: The terminal shows the device login URL and user code.
L114: 
L115: The QR code is hidden automatically when the terminal window is too small to render it without wrapping. The URL and code are always shown, so a narrow terminal never blocks login.
L116: 
L117: After login, Backboard R-CLI saves credentials locally so future sessions can start without another browser approval.
L118: 
L119: Useful auth commands:
L120: 
L121:     `backboard login
L122:     backboard logout
L123:     `
L124: Inside the interactive CLI, you can also type:
L125: 
L126:     `/login
L127:     /logout
L128:     `
L129: ## 【55†​】Create or open a project
L130: 
L131: R-CLI works inside a normal folder on your machine. You can use an existing repository:
L132: 
L133:     `cd /path/to/existing/repo
L134:     backboard
L135:     `
L136: 
L137: Or create a new project folder first:
L138: 
L139:     `mkdir my-app
L140:     cd my-app
L141:     git init
L142:     backboard
L143:     `
L144: 
L145: R-CLI does not require git — 【11†checkpoints】 let you undo file changes without it. Keeping your project in git is still recommended so you have a second layer of review.
L146: ## 【56†​】Start your first project session
L147: 
L148: Move into the project you want to work on:
L149: 
L150:     `cd /path/to/your/project
L151:     backboard
L152:     `
L153: 
L154: Or start from anywhere and point R-CLI at a folder:
L155: 
L156:     `backboard --cwd /path/to/your/project
L157:     `
L158: 
L159: 【57†Image: Backboard R-CLI welcome screen†storage.googleapis.com】
L160: 
L161: Backboard R-CLI opens inside the current workspace.
L162: The status bar at the bottom shows the current permission mode, the model, and the thinking mode:
L163: 
L164:     `⏸ Manual mode · (shift+tab to cycle) · openai/gpt-5.5 · medium
L165:     `
L166: 
L167: Press `Shift+Tab` at any time to cycle the permission mode. See 【10†Permissions】 for what each mode allows.
L168: ## 【58†​】Ask your first question
L169: 
L170: Type a normal request and press Enter:
L171: 
L172:     `Explain this project in simple terms.
L173:     `
L174: 
L175: For coding tasks, be direct:
L176: 
L177:     `Find the bug in the login page.
L178:     Add tests for the user settings form.
L179:     Refactor the upload handler to be easier to read.
L180:     `
L181: 
L182: 【59†Image: Backboard R-CLI first response†storage.googleapis.com】
L183: 
L184: A simple prompt and response in the terminal.
L185: R-CLI can read files, search the repo, edit files, run commands, use web search, fetch URLs, and ask you questions. Watch the terminal output so you know what it is doing.
L186: ## 【60†​】Steer or queue while R-CLI works
L187: 
L188: While a task is running, R-CLI shows `Tab to queue · Enter to steer` below the input box. You can keep typing without waiting for the turn to finish:
L189: 
L190: Action  | What it does
L191: --- | ---
L192: Press `Enter`  | Steer the current turn with new instructions
L193: Press `Tab`  | Queue your message for the next turn
L194: Press `Esc`  | Interrupt the current turn
L195: 
L196: The placeholder while busy reads `(working - press Ctrl+C to interrupt)`. Both `Esc` and `Ctrl+C` interrupt the turn.
L197: Steering is useful when you want to correct direction immediately:
L198: 
L199:     `Actually keep this change minimal and do not touch the API layer.
L200:     `
L201: 
L202: Queueing is useful when the agent is still working, but you already know the next thing you want:
L203: 
L204:     `After that, add a regression test for this case.
L205:     `
L206: ## 【61†​】Review changes safely
L207: 
L208: R-CLI records a checkpoint for every turn, so you can revert its edits directly:
L209: 
L210:     `/undo
L211:     `
L212: 
L213: See 【11†Checkpoints】 for the full undo, redo, and rewind flow.
L214: 
L215: You can also use git as a second layer:
L216: 
L217:     `git status
L218:     git diff
L219:     git restore path/to/file
L220:     `
L221: 
L222: Avoid broad cleanup commands unless you are sure they will not remove untracked work.
L223: ## 【62†​】Attach files
L224: 
L225: Drag files onto the terminal to attach them to your next message, or press `Ctrl+V` to attach an image from your clipboard. See 【14†Attachments】 for supported types and limits.
L226: ## 【63†​】One-shot mode
L227: 
L228: Use `--print` when you want one answer and then exit:
L229: 
L230:     `backboard --print "summarize this repo"
L231:     `
L232: 
L233: 【64†Image: Backboard R-CLI one-shot mode†storage.googleapis.com】
L234: 
L235: One-shot mode prints an answer and exits.
L236: 
L237: Useful one-shot patterns:
L238: 
L239:     `backboard --cwd /path/to/project --print "find the TODO comments"
L240:     backboard --format json --print "summarize this repo"
L241:     echo "summarize this repo" | backboard --format json
L242:     `
L243: `--print` runs non-interactively, so R-CLI cannot show permission prompts. Any tool call that would normally ask is denied automatically. Before scripting R-CLI, pre-approve the tools it needs in `.backboard/settings.json`, or pass `--permission-mode bypass`. See 【65†Permissions】.
L244: ## 【66†​】Troubleshooting
L245: 
L246: ### 【67†​】`backboard: command not found`
L247: 
L248: Restart your terminal, then run the install command again.
L249: 
L250: ### 【68†​】Login does not complete
L251: 
L252: Run:
L253: 
L254:     `backboard login
L255:     `
L256: 
L257: Open the printed URL in a browser where you can sign in to Backboard, or scan the QR code with your phone. Approve the device login, then return to the terminal.
L258: ### 【69†​】The agent changed a file unexpectedly
L259: 
L260: Revert the last turn:
L261: 
L262:     `/undo
L263:     `
L264: 
L265: Or inspect the diff first with `git diff`, then decide whether to keep it, edit it, or restore that file.
L266: 
L267: ### 【70†​】A tool call was denied automatically
L268: 
L269: You are running non-interactively, or a `deny` rule matched. See 【10†Permissions】.
L270: 
L271: ### 【71†​】File search does not work
L272: 
L273: Install `ripgrep`, also called `rg`.
L274: 
L275:   * ## macOS
L276: 
L277:   * ## Ubuntu / Debian
L278: 
L279:     `brew install ripgrep
L280:     `

L70: # Permissions
L71: 
L72: Control which tools R-CLI runs automatically, which ask first, and which are blocked outright.
L73: 
L74: Permissions decide what R-CLI may do without asking you. Read-only work runs freely; anything that changes your machine asks first, unless you have said otherwise.
L75: 
L76: By default R-CLI starts in Manual mode: it reads files and runs safe commands on its own, and asks before every edit, write, or non-trivial shell command.
L77: ## 【50†​】Permission modes
L78: 
L79: Press `Shift+Tab` to cycle modes during a session. The current mode is shown in the status bar.
L80: Mode  | Indicator  | Behavior
L81: --- | --- | ---
L82: `manual`  | `⏸ Manual`  | Default. Asks before anything that is not read-only or explicitly allowed.
L83: `acceptEdits`  | `◆ Accept Edits`  | File edits and writes inside your project folder run without asking. Shell commands and everything else still ask.
L84: `auto`  | `✦ Auto`  | Reserved for automatic classification. Today it behaves like `manual`.
L85: `bypass`  | `» Bypass`  | Runs everything except `deny` and `ask` rules. Not in the `Shift+Tab` cycle.
L86: Set the mode at startup instead:
L87: 
L88:     `backboard --permission-mode acceptEdits
L89:     `
L90: 
L91: `bypass` mode lets the agent run any command and edit any file without asking, including outside your project folder. Use it only in throwaway environments such as containers or CI. It is deliberately unreachable from `Shift+Tab` — you must pass the flag or set it in config.
L92: An unrecognized value does not stop the run. R-CLI falls back to `manual` and prints a warning:
L93: 
L94:     `Unknown --permission-mode "yolo"; using manual mode. Valid: manual, acceptEdits, auto, bypass.
L95:     `
L96: ## 【51†​】Configuration file
L97: 
L98: Permission settings live in your project, at the repository root:
L99: 
L100:     `<repo-root>/.backboard/settings.json
L101:     `
L102: The repo root is found by walking up from your working directory looking for `.git`, so every subdirectory of a project shares one policy.
L103: 
L104:     `{
L105:       "permissions": {
L106:         "mode": "manual",
L107:         "allow": [
L108:           "execute(git status:*)",
L109:           "execute(bun test:*)",
L110:           "read(src/**)"
L111:         ],
L112:         "deny": [
L113:           "execute(rm:*)",
L114:           "write(.env)"
L115:         ],
L116:         "ask": [
L117:           "execute(git push:*)"
L118:         ]
L119:       }
L120:     }
L121:     `
L122: Key  | Type  | Description
L123: --- | --- | ---
L124: `mode`  | string  | Starting permission mode. Overridden by `--permission-mode`.
L125: `allow`  | string[]  | Rules that run without asking.
L126: `deny`  | string[]  | Rules that are always blocked.
L127: `ask`  | string[]  | Rules that always prompt, even in `bypass` mode.
L128: 
L129: Mode precedence is `--permission-mode` flag, then `permissions.mode`, then `manual`.
L130: A missing or malformed `settings.json` is treated as empty settings — R-CLI falls back to defaults rather than failing to start.
L131: ## 【52†​】Rule syntax
L132: 
L133: A rule is a tool name, optionally followed by a pattern in parentheses:
L134: 
L135:     `execute                      # the whole Execute tool
L136:     execute(git status:*)        # commands starting with "git status"
L137:     write(.env)                  # writing exactly .env
L138:     read(src/**)                 # reading anything under src/
L139:     `
L140: 
L141: Tool names are lower-cased, for example `execute`, `read`, `write`, `edit`, `find_skill`, `find_mcp`.
L142: Patterns are matched against the meaningful part of the call — the command string for `execute`, the file path for `edit` and `write`:
L143: 
L144: Pattern form  | Matches
L145: --- | ---
L146: `prefix:*`  | Content equal to `prefix`, or starting with `prefix` followed by a space
L147: Contains `*`  | Glob match, for example `read(src/**)`
L148: Anything else  | Exact string equality
L149: `prefix:*` matches on whole space-delimited tokens, not raw text. `execute(git:*)` allows every `git` subcommand, including `git push` and `git reset --hard`. Scope allow rules as tightly as you can.
L150: ## 【53†​】How a decision is made
L151: 
L152: For every tool call, the first matching step wins:
L153: 
L154: 1
L155: 
L156: ### Deny rule
L157: 
L158: A matching `deny` rule blocks the call. Nothing overrides this.
L159: 
L160: 2
L161: 
L162: ### Ask rule
L163: 
L164: A matching `ask` rule always prompts, even in `bypass` mode.
L165: 
L166: 3
L167: ### Tool verdict
L168: 
L169: Some tools decide for themselves. In `acceptEdits` mode, `Edit`, `Write`, and `ApplyPatch` approve paths inside the directory R-CLI was started in — not the whole repository. A symlink that resolves outside that directory is still rejected.
L170: 
L171: 4
L172: 
L173: ### Read-only check
L174: 
L175: Tools that only read are allowed automatically, in every mode.
L176: 
L177: 5
L178: 
L179: ### Bypass mode
L180: 
L181: In `bypass` mode, everything remaining is allowed.
L182: 
L183: 6
L184: 
L185: ### Allow rule
L186: 
L187: A matching `allow` rule permits the call.
L188: 
L189: 7
L190: ### Otherwise, ask
L191: 
L192: Anything unmatched prompts you.
L193: 
L194: `deny` and `ask` are evaluated before the bypass gate on purpose: no mode can skip them. This makes `deny` a reliable guardrail even in automated runs.
L195: ## 【54†​】Safe commands
L196: 
L197: Some read-only shell commands are approved automatically without a rule:
L198: 
L199:     `git status   git diff   git log   git show
L200:     ls   pwd   cat   head   tail   wc   which   echo
L201:     grep   rg   find
L202:     bun test   bun run typecheck
L203:     `
L204: 
L205: Read-only forms of `git branch` are also approved — `--list`, `--show-current`, `-a`, `-r`, `-v`, and their combinations.
L206: 
L207: These are treated as unsafe and will still prompt:
L208:   * Anything containing `$(`, a backtick, `>`, or `<`.
L209:   * Chained commands where any segment is not itself safe — segments are split on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `&`, and newlines.
L210:   * `find` with `-exec`, `-execdir`, `-ok`, `-okdir`, `-delete`, `-fprint`, `-fprintf`, `-fprint0`, or `-fls`.
L211:   * `rg` with `--pre`, `--pre-glob`, `--hostname-bin`, `--search-zip`, or `-z`.
L212:   * `git status`, `git diff`, `git log`, or `git show` with `--output`.
L213:   * `git branch` with anything other than read-only flags such as `--list` or `--show-current`. A bare branch name mutates, so it prompts.
L214:   * Background commands, which are never auto-approved by the safe list.
L215: Quotes are stripped before the `find`, `rg`, and `git` flag checks, so `'-delete'` cannot dodge the guard. The `$(`, backtick, `>`, and `<` check runs on the raw command.
L216: ## 【55†​】The permission prompt
L217: 
L218: When a call needs approval, R-CLI shows the tool, a one-line summary of what it will do, and three choices:
L219: 
L220: Choice  | Effect
L221: --- | ---
L222: `Yes, allow once`  | Runs this one call.
L223: `Yes, always allow (<rule>)`  | Runs it and saves the shown rule to `settings.json`.
L224: `No, deny`  | Blocks the call and tells the agent.
L225: 
L226: The “always allow” option always shows the exact rule it will save, so you can see how broad it is before accepting.
L227: 
L228: R-CLI scopes that rule conservatively:
L229: Command shape  | Saved rule
L230: --- | ---
L231: A single path-like argument  | Exact path, for example `write(src/index.ts)`
L232: A sensitive command  | The exact full command, never a prefix
L233: Anything else  | First two tokens, for example `execute(bun test:*)`
L234: Sensitive commands that never generalize include `rm`, `rmdir`, `mv`, `dd`, `mkfs`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`, `chgrp`, `curl`, `wget`, `kill`, `killall`, `pkill`, `sudo`, `su`, `git`, `docker`, `ssh`, `scp`, and `rsync`. Approving `rm -rf build` once will not allow `rm` in general.
L235: 
L236: This list is best-effort rather than exhaustive. Prefer an explicit `deny` rule for anything you never want run.
L237: ## 【56†​】Headless and automation
L238: 
L239: Non-interactive runs cannot show a prompt, so anything that would ask is denied:
L240: 
L241:     `Permission required for Execute — permission prompts are unavailable in this context.
L242:     `
L243: 
L244: This applies to `--print` one-shot mode. To script R-CLI, either pre-approve exactly what it needs:
L245: 
L246:     `{
L247:       "permissions": {
L248:         "allow": ["execute(bun test:*)", "execute(git diff:*)"],
L249:         "deny": ["execute(git push:*)"]
L250:       }
L251:     }
L252:     `
L253: Or, in a disposable environment only:
L254: 
L255:     `backboard --print "run the test suite" --permission-mode bypass
L256:     `
L257: 
L258: Pairing `bypass` with a `deny` list is safer than `bypass` alone. Deny rules still apply, so you can block destructive commands while letting everything else run unattended.
L259: ## 【57†​】Sub-agents
L260: 
L261: Sub-agents inherit the parent session’s mode and rules, but can never prompt. Each of their tool calls is checked individually, and anything that would ask is denied.
L262: 
L263: Sub-agents also cannot install third-party code. They can call the 【58†skill and MCP discovery tools】, but those tools refuse to install anything from a sub-agent and report the match back instead. Only the main agent can request an install, and only with your confirmation.
L264: ## 【59†​】Related
L265: 
L266:   * 【16†Command reference】 — the `--permission-mode` flag and config file locations

L268:   * 【12†Skills and discovery】 — confirmation before installing third-party skills and MCP servers

---BACKBOARD INSTALLER HEAD---
#!/bin/sh
# Backboard CLI installer (native binary)
# Usage: curl -fsSL https://app.backboard.io/api/cli | bash
set -eu

API_BASE="https://app.backboard.io/api"
INVITE_REQUIRED="0"
CODE=""

red()   { printf '\033[31m%s\033[0m\n' "$1" >&2; }
cyan()  { printf '\033[36m%s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }
green() { printf '\033[32m%s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }

# Pick the most specific binary slug for this box. x64 builds need AVX2
# (Haswell+); CPUs without it get the -baseline slice. Alpine/Void have no
# glibc, so they get the -musl slice. This mirrors Bun's own install.sh.
has_avx2_linux() { grep -qi '\bavx2\b' /proc/cpuinfo 2>/dev/null; }
has_avx2_macos() { sysctl -a 2>/dev/null | grep -i machdep.cpu | grep -qi avx2; }
is_musl() { [ -f /etc/alpine-release ] || (ldd --version 2>&1 | grep -qi musl); }

case "$(uname -s)" in
    Darwin)
        # `uname -m` reports the *current process* arch, which is
        # ``x86_64`` whenever the shell is running under Rosetta (a
        # common setup). The machine underneath may still be Apple
        # Silicon, and our arm64 binary runs there natively, so trust
        # the hardware probe (`hw.optional.arm64` is 1 on every Apple
        # Silicon Mac) over the translated process arch. Genuine Intel
        # Macs fall through to the x86_64 build.
        if [ "$(uname -m)" = "arm64" ] || [ "$(sysctl -n hw.optional.arm64 2>/dev/null)" = "1" ]; then
            PLATFORM="macos-arm64"
        elif has_avx2_macos; then
            PLATFORM="macos-x64"
        else
            PLATFORM="macos-x64-baseline"
        fi
        ;;
    Linux)
        LIBC=""
        if is_musl; then LIBC="-musl"; fi
        case "$(uname -m)" in
            aarch64|arm64) PLATFORM="linux-arm64${LIBC}" ;;
            x86_64|amd64)
                PLATFORM="linux-x64${LIBC}"
                has_avx2_linux || PLATFORM="${PLATFORM}-baseline"
                ;;
            *)
                red "error: unsupported Linux arch \"$(uname -m)\" — need arm64 or x86_64."
                exit 1
                ;;
        esac
        ;;
    *)
        red "error: unsupported OS \"$(uname -s)\" — use /cli/windows on Windows."
        exit 1
        ;;
esac

if [ "$INVITE_REQUIRED" = "1" ] && [ -z "$CODE" ]; then
    printf 'Enter your invite code: '
    read CODE < /dev/tty
fi

INSTALL_DIR="${BACKBOARD_INSTALL:-$HOME/.backboard}/bin"
BINARY="$INSTALL_DIR/backboard"
URL="$API_BASE/cli/download/$PLATFORM"
if [ -n "$CODE" ]; then
    URL="$URL?code=$CODE"
fi

mkdir -p "$INSTALL_DIR"
cyan "  downloading backboard ($PLATFORM)..."
if ! curl -fsSL "$URL" -o "$BINARY.tmp"; then
    red "error: download failed (invalid invite code, or binary not available for $PLATFORM)."
    rm -f "$BINARY.tmp"
    exit 1
fi
chmod +x "$BINARY.tmp"
mv "$BINARY.tmp" "$BINARY"

# Pick the rc files this user's shell actually reads. zsh on macOS
# reads .zshrc for interactive shells and .zprofile for login shells
# (a fresh Terminal.app window is a login shell), so write both —
# otherwise a new window still can't find `backboard`.
case "${SHELL:-}" in
    *zsh)  RC_FILES="$HOME/.zshrc $HOME/.zprofile"; RC="$HOME/.zshrc" ;;
    *bash) RC_FILES="$HOME/.bashrc $HOME/.bash_profile"; RC="$HOME/.bashrc" ;;
    *)     RC_FILES="$HOME/.profile"; RC="$HOME/.profile" ;;
esac

for rc in $RC_FILES; do
    if ! grep -q '.backboard/bin' "$rc" 2>/dev/null; then
        printf '\nexport PATH="%s:$PATH"\n' "$INSTALL_DIR" >> "$rc"
    fi
done

green "  installed -> $BINARY"

# A piped installer runs in a CHILD shell, so it can't mutate the PATH
# of the terminal the user is sitting in — editing rc files only helps
# FUTURE shells. To make a bare `backboard` work right now (no `source`,
# no new terminal), drop a symlink into the first writable, non-system
# directory that's already on the current $PATH. The child inherits the
# parent's $PATH, so this is the same set the parent resolves against.
RESIDENT=""
case ":$PATH:" in
    *":$INSTALL_DIR:"*) RESIDENT="$BINARY" ;;
    *)
        OLD_IFS="$IFS"
        IFS=":"
        for dir in $PATH; do
            IFS="$OLD_IFS"
            { [ -n "$dir" ] && [ -d "$dir" ] && [ -w "$dir" ]; } || { IFS=":"; continue; }
            # Never our own dir (self-referential link) and never system
            # dirs (fighting the OS/package managers breaks other tools).
            case "$dir" in
                "$INSTALL_DIR"|/bin|/sbin|/usr/bin|/usr/sbin|/var/*|/etc/*) IFS=":"; continue ;;
            esac
            # Don't clobber a real `backboard` from another tool, but do
            # replace a symlink (ours from a prior install, or a stale one).
            if [ -e "$dir/backboard" ] && [ ! -L "$dir/backboard" ]; then IFS=":"; continue; fi
            if ln -sf "$BINARY" "$dir/backboard" 2>/dev/null; then
                RESIDENT="$dir/backboard"
                cyan "  linked $dir/backboard (already on your PATH)"
                break
            fi
            IFS=":"
        done
        IFS="$OLD_IFS"
        ;;
esac

if [ -n "$RESIDENT" ]; then
    printf '  run: \033[36mbackboard\033[0m\n'
else
    # No writable PATH dir — the rc edit above still fixes future shells.
    printf '  added %s to PATH in %s\n' "$INSTALL_DIR" "$RC"
    printf '  run it now with:  \033[36msource %s && backboard\033[0m\n' "$RC"
    printf '  (or open a new terminal and run \033[36mbackboard\033[0m)\n'
fi

#!/bin/sh
# Backboard CLI installer (native binary)
# Usage: curl -fsSL https://app.backboard.io/api/cli | bash
set -eu

API_BASE="https://app.backboard.io/api"
INVITE_REQUIRED="0"
CODE=""

red()   { printf '\033[31m%s\033[0m\n' "$1" >&2; }
cyan()  { printf '\033[36m%s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }
green() { printf '\033[32m%s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }

# Pick the most specific binary slug for this box. x64 builds need AVX2
# (Haswell+); CPUs without it get the -baseline slice. Alpine/Void have no
# glibc, so they get the -musl slice. This mirrors Bun's own install.sh.
has_avx2_linux() { grep -qi '\bavx2\b' /proc/cpuinfo 2>/dev/null; }
has_avx2_macos() { sysctl -a 2>/dev/null | grep -i machdep.cpu | grep -qi avx2; }
is_musl() { [ -f /etc/alpine-release ] || (ldd --version 2>&1 | grep -qi musl); }

case "$(uname -s)" in
    Darwin)
        # `uname -m` reports the *current process* arch, which is
        # ``x86_64`` whenever the shell is running under Rosetta (a
        # common setup). The machine underneath may still be Apple
        # Silicon, and our arm64 binary runs there natively, so trust
        # the hardware probe (`hw.optional.arm64` is 1 on every Apple
        # Silicon Mac) over the translated process arch. Genuine Intel
        # Macs fall through to the x86_64 build.
        if [ "$(uname -m)" = "arm64" ] || [ "$(sysctl -n hw.optional.arm64 2>/dev/null)" = "1" ]; then
            PLATFORM="macos-arm64"
        elif has_avx2_macos; then
            PLATFORM="macos-x64"
        else
            PLATFORM="macos-x64-baseline"
        fi
        ;;
    Linux)
        LIBC=""
        if is_musl; then LIBC="-musl"; fi
        case "$(uname -m)" in
            aarch64|arm64) PLATFORM="linux-arm64${LIBC}" ;;
            x86_64|amd64)
                PLATFORM="linux-x64${LIBC}"
                has_avx2_linux || PLATFORM="${PLATFORM}-baseline"
                ;;
            *)
                red "error: unsupported Linux arch \"$(uname -m)\" — need arm64 or x86_64."
                exit 1
                ;;
        esac
        ;;
    *)
        red "error: unsupported OS \"$(uname -s)\" — use /cli/windows on Windows."
        exit 1
        ;;
esac

if [ "$INVITE_REQUIRED" = "1" ] && [ -z "$CODE" ]; then
    printf 'Enter your invite code: '
    read CODE < /dev/tty
fi

INSTALL_DIR="${BACKBOARD_INSTALL:-$HOME/.backboard}/bin"
BINARY="$INSTALL_DIR/backboard"
URL="$API_BASE/cli/download/$PLATFORM"
if [ -n "$CODE" ]; then
    URL="$URL?code=$CODE"
fi

mkdir -p "$INSTALL_DIR"
cyan "  downloading backboard ($PLATFORM)..."
if ! curl -fsSL "$URL" -o "$BINARY.tmp"; then
    red "error: download failed (invalid invite code, or binary not available for $PLATFORM)."
    rm -f "$BINARY.tmp"
    exit 1
fi
chmod +x "$BINARY.tmp"
mv "$BINARY.tmp" "$BINARY"

# Pick the rc files this user's shell actually reads. zsh on macOS
# reads .zshrc for interactive shells and .zprofile for login shells
# (a fresh Terminal.app window is a login shell), so write both —
# otherwise a new window still can't find `backboard`.
case "${SHELL:-}" in
    *zsh)  RC_FILES="$HOME/.zshrc $HOME/.zprofile"; RC="$HOME/.zshrc" ;;
    *bash) RC_FILES="$HOME/.bashrc $HOME/.bash_profile"; RC="$HOME/.bashrc" ;;
    *)     RC_FILES="$HOME/.profile"; RC="$HOME/.profile" ;;
esac

for rc in $RC_FILES; do
    if ! grep -q '.backboard/bin' "$rc" 2>/dev/null; then
        printf '\nexport PATH="%s:$PATH"\n' "$INSTALL_DIR" >> "$rc"
    fi
done

green "  installed -> $BINARY"

# A piped installer runs in a CHILD shell, so it can't mutate the PATH
# of the terminal the user is sitting in — editing rc files only helps
# FUTURE shells. To make a bare `backboard` work right now (no `source`,
# no new terminal), drop a symlink into the first writable, non-system
# directory that's already on the current $PATH. The child inherits the
# parent's $PATH, so this is the same set the parent resolves against.
RESIDENT=""
case ":$PATH:" in
    *":$INSTALL_DIR:"*) RESIDENT="$BINARY" ;;
    *)
        OLD_IFS="$IFS"
        IFS=":"
        for dir in $PATH; do
            IFS="$OLD_IFS"
            { [ -n "$dir" ] && [ -d "$dir" ] && [ -w "$dir" ]; } || { IFS=":"; continue; }
            # Never our own dir (self-referential link) and never system
            # dirs (fighting the OS/package managers breaks other tools).
            case "$dir" in
                "$INSTALL_DIR"|/bin|/sbin|/usr/bin|/usr/sbin|/var/*|/etc/*) IFS=":"; continue ;;
            esac
            # Don't clobber a real `backboard` from another tool, but do
            # replace a symlink (ours from a prior install, or a stale one).
            if [ -e "$dir/backboard" ] && [ ! -L "$dir/backboard" ]; then IFS=":"; continue; fi
            if ln -sf "$BINARY" "$dir/backboard" 2>/dev/null; then
                RESIDENT="$dir/backboard"
                cyan "  linked $dir/backboard (already on your PATH)"
                break
            fi
            IFS=":"
        done
        IFS="$OLD_IFS"
        ;;
esac

if [ -n "$RESIDENT" ]; then
    printf '  run: \033[36mbackboard\033[0m\n'
else
    # No writable PATH dir — the rc edit above still fixes future shells.
    printf '  added %s to PATH in %s\n' "$INSTALL_DIR" "$RC"
    printf '  run it now with:  \033[36msource %s && backboard\033[0m\n' "$RC"
    printf '  (or open a new terminal and run \033[36mbackboard\033[0m)\n'
fi

The SENSITIVE set is the part I'd invert. As written, the processor is still fail-open: safe() can be forgotten, and so can adding the next free-text key to SENSITIVE. If a teammate later records raw tool args or a handoff message under some new gen_ai.agent.* attribute, it exports before anyone notices. At the boundary I'd redact every string attribute by default, then keep a small ALLOWLIST for fields that are known-safe raw, like order_id, model name, token counts, tool name. Forget to classify a new key under that scheme and you lose some trace detail, you don't leak regulated data. That's the whole reason to centralize this in a processor.

I'd also be careful with decision.reason. If it's derived from the model's stated rationale, grouping eval trajectories on it scores self-report rather than behavior. A model can call the right tool and narrate a wrong reason. Keep decision.reason for debugging, and group on the decision plus the observable inputs it keyed off, like tool args or retrieved record ids.

The SENSITIVE set is the part I'd invert. As written, the processor is still fail-open: safe() can be forgotten, and so can adding the next free-text key to SENSITIVE. If a teammate later records raw tool args or a handoff message under some new gen_ai.agent.* attribute, it exports before anyone notices. At the boundary I'd redact every string attribute by default, then keep a small ALLOWLIST for fields that are known-safe raw, like order_id, model name, token counts, tool name. Forget to classify a new key under that scheme and you lose some trace detail, you don't leak regulated data. That's the whole reason to centralize this in a processor.

I'd also be careful with decision.reason. If it's derived from the model's stated rationale, grouping eval trajectories on it scores self-report rather than behavior. A model can call the right tool and narrate a wrong reason. Keep decision.reason for debugging, and group on the decision plus the observable inputs it keyed off, like tool args or retrieved record ids.

What I would add is where the allowlist lives - if it is a plain list in the processor, anyone shipping a new attribute can widen the safe set, so it is better as a short reviewed list plus a test that fails when an unclassified key shows up in a trace. The SENSITIVE set is the part I'd invert. As written, the processor is still fail-open: safe() can be forgotten, and so can adding the next free-text key to SENSITIVE. If a teammate later records raw tool args or a handoff message under some new gen_ai.agent.* attribute, it exports before anyone notices. At the boundary I'd redact every string attribute by default, then keep a small ALLOWLIST for fields that are known-safe raw, like order_id, model name, token counts, tool name. Forget to classify a new key under that scheme and you lose some trace detail, you don't leak regulated data. That's the whole reason to centralize this in a processor.

I'd also be careful with decision.reason. If it's derived from the model's stated rationale, grouping eval trajectories on it scores self-report rather than behavior. A model can call the right tool and narrate a wrong reason. Keep decision.reason for debugging, and group on the decision plus the observable inputs it keyed off, like tool args or retrieved record ids.
